key_works: Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities; Zhou et al. (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*.

title: Cryogenic target injection
open: Inject cryogenic targets through the chamber while preserving layer quality, orientation, and dimensional tolerances.
status: IFE studies specify demanding injection speeds and precision; integrated reactor-chamber qualification remains open.
why: A perfect stationary target may be damaged before reaching the shot point.
key_works: Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*.

title: Real-time target tracking and beam interception
open: Track moving targets and steer all driver beams with sufficiently low error despite chamber light, debris, vibration, and thermal distortion.
status: Tracking requirements are identified in IFE development plans; a complete power-plant environment remains unqualified.
why: Small positioning errors translate directly into failed or asymmetric implosions.
key_works: Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities; Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.

title: Chamber clearing between shots
open: Remove or redistribute vapor, ions, aerosols, and debris quickly enough that the next target and driver pulse encounter acceptable conditions.
status: Chamber concepts exist; high-yield repetitive clearing is a distinct unproven systems requirement.
why: Residual chamber material can ruin coupling and target survival.
key_works: Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*; Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Stable protective liquid-wall jets
open: Maintain the required liquid-jet geometry through repeated neutron, photon, shock, and vapor loading while preserving beam and target access.
status: Liquid protection is a longstanding chamber approach; integrated repetitive fusion qualification remains open.
why: Liquid walls could reduce solid-component damage and replacement frequency.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*.

title: Dry-wall cyclic survival
open: Qualify dry chamber surfaces for the combined cyclic thermal shock, implantation, sputtering, and neutron damage of a specified IFE design.
status: Materials studies characterize individual loads; complete repetitive exposure remains unqualified.
why: Average heat flux can conceal destructive pulse-by-pulse fatigue.
key_works: Knaster, Moeslang, and Muroga (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Low-inventory IFE target fuel cycle
open: Keep tritium inventory and losses acceptable across target filling, layering, storage, injection, failed shots, and chamber recovery.
status: General tritium technology exists, but consumable-target logistics add distinct inventory and recovery problems.
why: A high-gain target system can still fail fuel-self-sufficiency or safety requirements.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99; Ma (2023).

title: High-gain repetitive campaign reliability
open: Demonstrate a statistically meaningful sequence of high-gain shots at relevant repetition, including failures, recovery time, and component degradation.
status: Repeated ignition shots have been reported, but this is not equivalent to an industrial-duty campaign.
why: Plant economics depend on successful shots per operating hour, not the best shot.
key_works: LLNL (2026), *Meet the Machines That Matter: The Optics Inspector*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Target-debris recycling
open: Recover useful target and chamber materials from activated mixed debris with acceptable waste volume, tritium loss, and processing cost.
status: IFE development identifies chamber and fuel-cycle needs; integrated industrial recycling remains unresolved.
why: Consumable targets create continuous material flows that must be included in plant economics.
key_works: Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities; Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*.

title: Positive complete-system proton–boron power balance
open: Demonstrate a proton–boron-11 system whose fusion output exceeds all losses and sustainment costs under a transparently defined boundary.
status: Magnetically confined p–¹¹B reactions were measured in 2023; this did not establish net energy.
why: It is the decisive test for a widely discussed low-neutron fusion route.
key_works: Magee et al. (2023), *First measurements of p11B fusion in a magnetically confined plasma*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-36655-1.

title: Proton–boron reactivity uncertainty
open: Produce a reconciled, uncertainty-quantified p–¹¹B reaction dataset and determine its consequences for realistic distribution functions and energy balance.
status: A 2026 reassessment revisits cross-sections, reactivity, and energy balance; uncertainty-sensitive design conclusions remain active.
why: Small changes in a difficult fuel’s reactivity can materially alter feasibility claims.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026), *Revisiting p-11B Fusion: Updated Cross-sections, Reactivity, and Energy Balance*, arXiv:2601.00241.

title: Proton–boron alpha-ash management
open: Remove or beneficially use the three-alpha reaction products without losing the fuel distributions needed for favorable p–¹¹B performance.
status: Alpha-channeling schemes improve modeled balances, but experimentally validated ash handling remains open.
why: Product accumulation and thermalization can undermine proposed nonequilibrium advantages.
key_works: Ochs et al. (2022), *Improving the Feasibility of Economical Proton-Boron 11 Fusion via Alpha Channeling with a Hybrid Fast and Thermal Proton Scheme*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.106.055215.

title: Nonequilibrium fusion maintenance bounds
open: Establish sharp bounds on the power needed to maintain useful non-Maxwellian distributions, including proposed wave-driven or selectively heated exceptions.
status: Rider established important limitations in 1997 under stated assumptions; proposed new architectures must be assessed without ignoring those assumptions.
why: Apparent reactivity advantages can disappear when distribution-maintenance power is counted.
key_works: Rider (1997), *Fundamental limitations on plasma fusion systems not in thermodynamic equilibrium*, DOI: 10.1063/1.872556.

title: Practical catalyzed deuterium–deuterium cycles
open: Demonstrate a D–D-based cycle that productively burns or manages its tritium and helium-3 intermediates with acceptable confinement and processing requirements.
status: Reaction pathways are known; practical complete-cycle gain remains unresolved.
why: It could reduce dependence on externally supplied tritium while introducing harder plasma conditions.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990.

title: Sustainable helium-3 fuel supply
open: Establish a credible terrestrial supply, production, or recovery pathway for a specified D–³He deployment scale, including energy and cost accounting.
status: D–³He remains an alternative-fuel concept; fuel availability is a separate unresolved deployment constraint.
why: A favorable plasma design is not deployable without a realistic fuel supply.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Polarization survival in fusion fuel
open: Preserve useful nuclear-spin polarization through production, storage, injection, ionization, and confinement.
status: Ab initio calculations predict polarized D–T benefits; maintaining the polarization in an operating fusion system remains distinct.
why: Theoretical cross-section gains are irrelevant if polarization is rapidly lost.
key_works: Hupin, Quaglioni, and Navrátil (2019), *Ab initio predictions for polarized deuterium-tritium thermonuclear fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-08052-6.

title: Polarized-fusion reaction validation
open: Measure polarization-dependent reactivity and angular distributions with sufficient precision to validate reactor-relevant nuclear calculations.
status: Predictive calculations exist; complete experimentally constrained reactor inputs remain open.
why: Directional products and enhanced reactivity could affect both performance and shielding.
key_works: Hupin et al. (2019), *Ab initio predictions for polarized deuterium-tritium thermonuclear fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-08052-6.

title: Economical muon production
open: Produce and deliver useful stopped muons with an energy cost low enough for a complete muon-catalyzed fusion cycle to have positive net output.
status: Muon-catalyzed fusion is established physics; production efficiency remains a central energy-system bottleneck.
why: Catalysis cannot yield useful power if making the catalyst consumes too much energy.
key_works: Yin, Kou, and Chen (2026), *Muon-Catalyzed Nuclear Fusion: Physical Mechanism, Bottleneck Breakthroughs, and an Engineering Pathway*, arXiv:2605.26432.

title: Muon sticking and reactivation control
open: Increase useful fusion cycles per muon through experimentally validated control of sticking, reactivation, molecular formation, and decay losses.
status: Molecular and catalytic processes have direct experimental study; proposed large cycle-count improvements should not be treated as achieved records.
why: Catalyst lifetime is a fundamental determinant of complete-system feasibility.
key_works: Yin et al. (2026), *Muon-Catalyzed Nuclear Fusion: Physical Mechanism, Bottleneck Breakthroughs, and an Engineering Pathway*, arXiv:2605.26432; Toyama et al. (2026), DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3321.

title: REBCO performance under fusion irradiation
open: Qualify critical current, mechanical integrity, and thermal behavior of REBCO conductors under the relevant neutron spectrum and accumulated dose.
status: The SPARC model-coil program demonstrated high-field engineering; it did not establish full fusion-irradiation lifetime.
why: Magnet compactness is useful only if the conductor survives the neutron environment.
key_works: Hartwig et al. (2024), *The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program*, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613; Knaster et al. (2016), DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: REBCO strain and fatigue lifetime
open: Predict conductor degradation under combined cyclic strain, transverse stress, thermal cycling, and irradiation.
status: Large high-field coils have been built and tested; long-term coupled-load lifetime remains separate.
why: Local conductor damage can limit an entire magnet system.
key_works: Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Early HTS quench detection
open: Detect damaging local disturbances before hot spots become irreversible, despite slow normal-zone propagation and large electromagnetic backgrounds.
status: SPARC model-coil quench studies provide important evidence; reactor-wide detection guarantees remain unresolved.
why: A small undetected defect can destroy expensive stored-energy hardware.
key_works: SPARC TFMC collaboration (2024), *Quench Response of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Safe HTS energy extraction
open: Discharge a reactor magnet’s stored energy without excessive voltage, hot-spot temperature, mechanical shock, or damage to neighboring coils.
status: Model-coil tests address quench response, but complete reactor protection is a larger systems problem.
why: High magnetic energy increases the consequences of protection failure.
key_works: *Quench Response of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil* (2024); Hartwig et al. (2024), DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613.

title: Low-loss reactor magnet joints
open: Achieve predictable joint resistance and thermal stability across production variability, mechanical loading, and irradiation.
status: High-field coil fabrication demonstrates practical joints; reactor lifetime and population-level reliability remain open.
why: Small resistive losses at cryogenic temperature carry large electrical penalties.
key_works: Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Repeatedly demountable HTS joints
open: Repeatedly disconnect and reconnect reactor magnet joints while preserving electrical, mechanical, and vacuum performance.
status: Demountable magnets are a prominent compact-reactor design feature; lifecycle qualification remains unresolved.
why: Demountability could transform maintenance access, but only if joints remain reliable.
key_works: Sorbom et al. (2015), *ARC: A compact, high-field, fusion nuclear science facility and demonstration power plant with demountable magnets*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.008; Hartwig et al. (2024).

title: Radiation-resistant magnet insulation
open: Qualify insulating systems against combined radiation, cryogenic cycling, mechanical stress, and high-voltage events.
status: Fusion materials research identifies combined-environment testing as essential; a universal reactor-qualified insulation system does not follow.
why: Insulation failure can disable a magnet even when the superconductor remains functional.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Acceptable HTS alternating-current losses
open: Limit conductor and structural losses during ramps, control transients, and pulsed operation without sacrificing current capacity or protection.
status: High-field demonstrations establish feasibility of components, not every reactor waveform and duty cycle.
why: Dynamic losses increase cryogenic power and may constrain plasma control.
key_works: Hartwig et al. (2024), *The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program*, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613.

title: Industrial REBCO quality and scale
open: Supply long conductor lengths with verified uniformity, traceability, repairability, and reactor-relevant acceptance testing.
status: The SPARC model coil used hundreds of kilometers of tape; scaling that achievement into a reliable fleet supply chain remains distinct.
why: Rare local defects become consequential in very long conductor inventories.
key_works: Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Fusion-plant cryogenic availability
open: Demonstrate cryogenic systems whose efficiency, redundancy, maintenance, and recovery times meet complete-plant availability requirements.
status: Large cryogenic systems exist, but fusion-specific integrated availability remains a development objective.
why: A small cold-system fault can interrupt a much larger generating asset.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Ductile tungsten operating window
open: Develop tungsten-based plasma-facing materials that retain adequate toughness across fabrication, startup, operation, irradiation, and shutdown.
status: Tungsten brittleness and processing were major issues in the 2013 European review; coupled reactor qualification remains open.
why: A material can withstand heat yet fail by cracking.
key_works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Predictive tungsten erosion lifetime
open: Predict net tungsten erosion and redeposition under realistic mixed-species plasma exposure, transients, and evolving surface morphology.
status: Sputtering and redeposition are extensively studied; lifetime prediction under combined reactor conditions remains uncertain.
why: Erosion determines component life and plasma contamination.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.

title: Helium-induced tungsten morphology
open: Determine when helium bubbles, roughening, and fuzz form under reactor exposure and how they affect erosion, thermal response, and dust.
status: Helium-implantation experiments establish major mechanisms; extrapolation to simultaneous neutron and mixed-plasma loading remains open.
why: Surface morphology can change faster than bulk material properties.
key_works: Hofmann et al. (2017), *Helium-Ion-Implantation in Tungsten: Progress towards a…* (full title verify); Rieth et al. (2013), DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Tritium trapping in damaged tungsten
open: Predict and measure tritium retention in tungsten with realistic neutron defects, helium, impurities, temperature cycles, and plasma exposure.
status: Retention mechanisms are established; coupled-condition inventory prediction remains uncertain.
why: Retention affects fuel availability, safety, and component disposal.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218; Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*.

title: Tungsten recrystallization under service loads
open: Control recrystallization, grain growth, and resulting loss of strength during long high-temperature service with irradiation.
status: Recrystallization is a longstanding tungsten-development concern; reactor lifetime depends on coupled thermal and irradiation history.
why: Acceptable initial properties may not survive prolonged operation.
key_works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Tungsten transmutation effects
open: Predict how neutron-driven composition changes alter tungsten thermal conductivity, toughness, swelling, and hydrogen retention.
status: Fusion materials research identifies transmutation as a distinctive challenge; full lifetime property evolution remains incompletely validated.
why: The material’s composition changes while the reactor operates.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; Zinkle and Snead (2014), DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Durable tungsten-to-heat-sink joints
open: Qualify joints against thermal-expansion mismatch, high heat flux, irradiation, cyclic loading, and manufacturing defects.
status: Plasma-facing joining technology has advanced; complete reactor-duty qualification remains unresolved.
why: The joint may fail before either bulk material reaches its limit.
key_works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Melt-layer motion and resolidification
open: Predict molten surface motion, ejection, electrical forces, and post-event geometry during extreme plasma transients.
status: Melting and material redistribution are recognized damage mechanisms; validated reactor-scale predictions remain difficult.
why: A brief melt event can create a permanent geometry defect that worsens later heating.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.

title: Liquid-metal surface contamination control
open: Maintain a liquid-metal plasma-facing surface without unacceptable vapor, droplets, or impurity transport into the confined plasma.
status: Liquid surfaces offer self-renewal, but plasma compatibility remains an independent qualification issue.
why: Solving solid-wall erosion can create a more severe plasma-contamination problem.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Liquid-metal wetting and replenishment
open: Sustain uniform wetting and replenishment under magnetic fields, thermal gradients, plasma pressure, and evolving substrate chemistry.
status: Liquid-metal engineering studies identify strong coupling among flow, materials, and magnetohydrodynamics.
why: Dry spots defeat the protection offered by a nominally liquid-covered wall.
key_works: Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*.

title: Low-temperature RAFM embrittlement
open: Qualify reduced-activation ferritic–martensitic steels against neutron-induced hardening and embrittlement at the lower end of their service-temperature range.
status: Radiation-resistant alloy development is mature research, but complete fusion-spectrum qualification remains incomplete.
why: The usable temperature window constrains cooling and thermal efficiency.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: High-temperature RAFM creep strength
open: Extend or reliably qualify the upper-temperature operating window without unacceptable creep, microstructural instability, or irradiation effects.
status: Existing steels face competing low-temperature embrittlement and high-temperature strength constraints.
why: Higher coolant temperature improves conversion efficiency but stresses structural materials.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Large-scale ODS fabrication and joining
open: Manufacture and join oxide-dispersion-strengthened structural components while preserving beneficial nanostructure and irradiation performance.
status: ODS materials show promising radiation tolerance; component-scale processing remains a separate barrier.
why: Coupon-level properties do not automatically survive welding and industrial fabrication.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627; Lu et al. (2017), ODS irradiation study, PMCID: PMC5228121.

title: Irradiation-tolerant SiC composite joints
open: Qualify SiC/SiC joints and seals for mechanical integrity, hermeticity, thermal cycling, and neutron exposure.
status: SiC composites have a substantial nuclear-materials research history; joint and component qualification remain limiting.
why: A strong composite is insufficient if its joints leak or fail.
key_works: Katoh et al. (2007), *Assessment of Silicon Carbide Composites for Advanced Salt-Cooled Reactors*; Ozawa et al. (2007), *Mechanical properties of advanced SiC/SiC composites…* (full title verify).

title: Irradiated SiC thermal conductivity
open: Predict and preserve heat conduction through SiC composites after defect accumulation, interface evolution, and transmutation-gas production.
status: Irradiation effects are measured in selected conditions; full fusion-component thermal qualification remains open.
why: Conductivity loss can cause overheating even when mechanical strength remains acceptable.
key_works: Katoh et al. (2007), *Assessment of Silicon Carbide Composites for Advanced Salt-Cooled Reactors*; Knaster et al. (2016), DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Vanadium-alloy impurity tolerance
open: Establish acceptable oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and corrosion-product levels for vanadium alloys under realistic fabrication and service conditions.
status: Alternative low-activation alloys remain research candidates; environmental sensitivity complicates practical qualification.
why: Attractive intrinsic properties can be lost through trace contamination.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Helium–hydrogen–displacement synergy
open: Quantify how simultaneous helium, hydrogen, and displacement damage differ from the sum of separate exposures.
status: Radiation-resistant design principles exist, but reproducing and extrapolating coupled fusion damage remains a central qualification issue.
why: Single-effect tests can systematically mispredict service behavior.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Microstructure-to-component lifetime prediction
open: Connect defect production and microstructural evolution to engineering properties and component failure with quantified uncertainty.
status: Multiscale methods exist, but the complete predictive chain remains incompletely validated.
why: Without this connection, atomistic insight cannot reliably reduce qualification time.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Irradiation creep–fatigue–fracture interaction
open: Develop validated lifetime rules for structures experiencing irradiation, cyclic thermal stress, creep, and crack growth simultaneously.
status: Individual mechanisms are studied; fusion components require combined-load extrapolation beyond simple damage summation.
why: Maintenance intervals depend on the actual interaction of failure mechanisms.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; Rieth et al. (2013), DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Corrosion under simultaneous irradiation
open: Measure how irradiation changes corrosion, mass transfer, and cracking in blanket structural materials under flowing coolant.
status: Flowing-liquid and radiation studies exist separately; their coupling remains difficult to reproduce.
why: Radiation can change both the material and the chemistry attacking it.
key_works: Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*; Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Reliable fusion-spectrum irradiation sources
open: Provide sustained high-flux irradiation with a sufficiently representative fusion spectrum, usable test volume, and reliable specimen temperature control.
status: Materials reviews identify this infrastructure gap; accelerator-driven source concepts address it but do not eliminate all qualification needs.
why: Structural lifetime cannot be established solely from nonrepresentative irradiation.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Surrogate-irradiation equivalence
open: Establish when ion, fission-neutron, and accelerator exposures can predict fusion-neutron behavior, with explicit error bounds and failure conditions.
status: Surrogates accelerate research, but differences in spectrum, dose rate, gas production, and damage geometry remain consequential.
why: Reliable equivalence could greatly accelerate qualification; unjustified equivalence could invalidate it.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Small-specimen-to-component transfer
open: Infer component-scale toughness, fatigue, and failure distributions from the small specimens available in high-flux irradiation volumes.
status: Limited irradiation volume makes small-specimen testing attractive; scale transfer remains a qualification problem.
why: Reactor components cannot all be irradiated at full scale before deployment.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Fusion gas-production nuclear data
open: Reduce discrepancies and uncertainties in helium- and hydrogen-production cross-sections for important structural and functional materials.
status: The 2024 FENDL paper identifies remaining gas-production differences and validation needs.
why: Gas production changes embrittlement, swelling, and irradiation equivalence.
key_works: Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001; arXiv:2311.10063.

title: Activation and decay-data uncertainty
open: Provide validated activation and decay datasets, including covariances, sufficient for waste classification, maintenance dose, and accident analysis.
status: FENDL and associated activation efforts exist; remaining validation and covariance gaps are explicitly documented.
why: Uncertainty propagates into safety, maintenance, and disposal decisions.
key_works: Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001; WANDA nuclear-data workshop (2024).

title: Streaming through realistic penetrations
open: Validate neutron and gamma transport through complex ports, ducts, gaps, joints, and evolving maintenance configurations.
status: Transport codes and libraries are established; realistic three-dimensional benchmark coverage remains incomplete.
why: Small penetrations can dominate local dose and magnet damage.
key_works: Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001.

title: Better-than-dpa damage metrics
open: Develop practical irradiation descriptors that predict engineering property changes more reliably than displacement-per-atom totals alone.
status: Radiation-resistant materials research recognizes that defect survival, gas production, and microstructure matter beyond a scalar exposure measure.
why: A better metric would improve experiment comparison and lifetime extrapolation.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Joint irradiation-property benchmark database
open: Assemble traceable datasets connecting composition, processing, irradiation history, microstructure, and measured engineering properties, including negative results.
status: Materials databases exist; the proposed gap is comprehensive interoperable linkage and reproducible uncertainty, not the absence of all data.
why: Fragmented records obstruct qualification and machine-learning generalization.
key_works: Hosemann et al. (2018), *Materials selection for nuclear applications*; Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*.

title: Uncertainty-qualified tritium breeding margin
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Demonstrate that a complete as-built plant breeds enough recoverable tritium after accounting for ports, structures, losses, decay, reserve requirements, and uncertainty.
status: Fuel-self-sufficiency analyses show why a nominal breeding ratio above one is insufficient.
why: A plant can consume its fuel supply despite an attractive idealized neutronics result.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2021), *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35.

title: Integral blanket breeding validation
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Validate complete blanket predictions through experiments that couple neutron multiplication, breeding, heat removal, extraction, and structural effects.
status: Blanket concepts and component studies are extensive; integrated reactor-environment validation remains a major gap.
why: Separate subsystem tests can miss interactions that reduce recoverable breeding.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Three-dimensional liquid-metal MHD pressure drop
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Predict pressure loss and flow maldistribution through realistic blanket manifolds, bends, field gradients, and electrically coupled channels.
status: Prototypical experiments and modeling exist; general reactor-scale predictive accuracy remains incomplete.
why: Excessive pressure drop increases pumping power and structural loads.
key_works: Rhodes et al. (2021), *Pressure drop in a prototypical 3D magnetohydrodynamic…* (full title verify), OSTI:1773976; Smolentsev et al. (2017), *Review of recent MHD activities for liquid metal blankets in the US*.

title: Flow-channel-insert lifetime
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Qualify electrically insulating inserts against cracking, irradiation, thermal gradients, leakage currents, and coolant infiltration.
status: Inserts are a proposed route to reduce liquid-metal MHD losses; their coupled-environment lifetime remains unresolved.
why: A small insulation failure can change the entire hydraulic behavior of a blanket channel.
key_works: Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*.

title: Lead–lithium corrosion and mass transfer
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Predict long-term dissolution, deposition, plugging, and composition changes in flowing lead–lithium under magnetic and thermal gradients.
status: Dedicated MHD and corrosion facilities exist; reactor-duration extrapolation remains uncertain.
why: Corrosion can thin structures while deposition blocks remote parts of the loop.
key_works: Saeidi and Smolentsev (2014), *Numerical study of the effect of a magnetic field on corrosion of ferritic/martensitic steel in a turbulent PbLi flow*.

title: FLiBe redox and impurity control
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Maintain molten-salt chemistry that limits corrosion and supports tritium extraction despite irradiation and continuous material exchange.
status: Salt blanket concepts are established design options; their complete chemistry-control envelope remains unresolved.
why: Breeding, corrosion, extraction, and maintenance depend on the same evolving chemistry.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Tritium transport in molten-salt blankets
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Measure and predict tritium speciation, solubility, diffusion, trapping, and interfacial transfer over realistic salt chemistry and irradiation conditions.
status: Tritium transport models exist, but outer-cycle extraction and inventory predictions remain sensitive to uncertain properties.
why: Slow recovery can make an otherwise adequate breeder fuel-starved.
key_works: Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647.

title: Ceramic-breeder tritium-release kinetics
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Predict tritium release from evolving ceramic breeder microstructures under irradiation, thermal gradients, and purge-gas chemistry.
status: Solid-breeder concepts have extensive development history; recoverable breeding depends on release kinetics, not neutron production alone.
why: Tritium trapped in breeder material is unavailable to fuel the plasma.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Breeder-pebble bed evolution
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Predict crushing, rearrangement, sintering, contact conductance, and purge-flow changes in irradiated breeder beds.
status: Pebble-bed designs are established blanket candidates; coupled long-term mechanical and thermal evolution remains uncertain.
why: A bed can lose cooling or release performance without an obvious bulk structural failure.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Neutron-multiplier material lifetime
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Qualify multiplier materials against swelling, gas generation, chemical reactivity, thermal cycling, and recovery or disposal requirements.
status: Multiplier choices improve breeding but introduce material-specific lifetime and safety tradeoffs.
why: Breeding enhancement is useful only if the multiplier remains serviceable.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.

title: Low-parasitic-power helium cooling
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Remove blanket heat with helium while keeping pumping power, pressure-boundary stress, leakage, and heat-transfer margins acceptable.
status: Helium-cooled blanket concepts exist; the full efficiency–materials–pressure tradeoff remains design-limiting.
why: High pumping power can consume a substantial share of generated electricity.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Blanket transient survivability
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Demonstrate acceptable response to loss of flow, pressure excursions, plasma transients, and electromagnetic forcing without cascading blanket failure.
status: A 2025 study explicitly examines transient-plasma effects on liquid-metal blanket flows; integrated accident qualification remains broader.
why: Steady-state thermal adequacy does not establish safe transient behavior.
key_works: Smolentsev (2025), *A model and assessments of the effect of transient plasma on liquid metal flows in a fusion blanket*.

title: Startup tritium for a growing fleet
open: Establish a credible, timed supply of startup tritium for multiple plants, including competing demand, decay, reserves, and breeding ramp-up.
status: The supply problem was analyzed explicitly in 2018; individual self-sufficiency does not automatically imply fleet growth.
why: Plants may be technically ready but unable to obtain their initial fuel.
key_works: Pearson, Antoniazzi, and Nuttall (2018), *Tritium supply and use: a key issue for the development of nuclear fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.

title: High effective tritium burn fraction
open: Increase the fraction of injected tritium ultimately burned while maintaining plasma performance and manageable recycling.
status: Fuel-cycle analyses show that low burn fraction drives throughput and inventory requirements.
why: Better burn efficiency relaxes multiple downstream systems simultaneously.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2021), *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35.

title: Fast, low-inventory isotope separation
open: Separate hydrogen isotopes at required throughput while minimizing holdup, energy, contamination sensitivity, and recovery time.
status: Separation technologies exist; power-plant inventory and availability requirements remain demanding.
why: Fuel tied up in processing is unavailable for operation or new plants.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.

title: Rapid outer-cycle tritium recovery
open: Recover bred tritium from blanket fluids or solids quickly enough to satisfy dynamic fuel-self-sufficiency requirements.
status: ARC- and STEP-class models published in 2023 show the importance of coupled inventories and processing times.
why: A favorable long-run breeding ratio can coexist with short-run fuel starvation.
key_works: Meschini et al. (2023), *Modeling and analysis of the tritium fuel cycle for ARC- and STEP-class D-T fusion power plants*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/acf3fc.

title: Durable tritium permeation barriers
open: Qualify barriers against radiation, corrosion, thermal cycling, defects, and repair while maintaining sufficiently low tritium permeation.
status: Barrier and membrane approaches exist; coupled-environment durability remains unresolved.
why: Permeation affects fuel loss, worker exposure, and contamination of power-conversion systems.
key_works: Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Glugla et al. (2023 report).

title: Tritium-isotopologue property database
open: Establish experimentally constrained thermophysical and transport properties for tritium-bearing mixtures over fuel-cycle operating conditions.
status: A 2023 study calculates pure-isotopologue thermodynamic properties; broader mixtures and uncertainty validation remain open.
why: Process designs can be sensitive to extrapolated hydrogen-isotope properties.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *Thermodynamic property calculation for pure component hydrogen isotopologues considering tritium processing technologies in fusion fuel cycle*, *Fusion Engineering and Design* 197, 114059.

title: Real-time whole-plant tritium accounting
open: Locate and quantify tritium throughout a plant with uncertainty small enough for fuel management, leak detection, and safety decisions.
status: Accounting methods exist, but distributed retention and inaccessible inventories complicate a closed real-time balance.
why: An unexplained inventory deficit can mean fuel loss, hidden retention, or leakage.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647.

title: Rapid accident detritiation
open: Demonstrate reliable detritiation after representative releases, including water, surfaces, aerosols, and inaccessible equipment.
status: Detritiation technology exists; plant-specific transient performance and recovery remain qualification problems.
why: Release consequences and restart time depend on cleanup effectiveness.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.

title: Long-life tritium storage and getters
open: Qualify storage materials and systems against cycling, contamination, aging, helium-3 buildup, and abnormal thermal conditions.
status: Tritium storage is established technology; plant-scale lifecycle and inventory optimization remain unresolved.
why: Storage is both an operational buffer and a concentrated hazard.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; Pearson et al. (2018), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.

title: Continuous fusion exhaust pumping
open: Pump fuel, helium, impurities, and reactive species at reactor throughput with low inventory and little interruption for regeneration.
status: Advanced DT exhaust pumping was reviewed in 2014; continuous high-availability integration remains a development problem.
why: Pumping limits propagate into confinement, fuel inventory, and plant uptime.
key_works: Day and Giegerich (2014), *Development of Advanced Exhaust Pumping Technology for a DT Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1109/TPS.2014.2307435.

title: Minimum diagnostic set for safe burn control
open: Determine which measurements are necessary and sufficient to control a burning plasma safely when diagnostic access is strongly restricted.
status: Research machines use extensive diagnostics; reactor observability under shielding and lifetime constraints remains unresolved.
why: A controller cannot compensate for fundamentally unobservable dangerous states.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005; Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*.

title: Three-dimensional neutron-source reconstruction
open: Reconstruct fusion-source shape and motion with quantified uncertainty from sparse neutron and complementary diagnostics.
status: Three-dimensional multimodal reconstruction has advanced in ICF, including 2024–2025 studies; sparse-view ambiguity remains.
why: Apparent temperature or yield changes may actually reflect geometry or flow.
key_works: Kunimune et al. (2024), *3D reconstruction of an inertial-confinement fusion implosion with neural networks using multiple heterogeneous data sources*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0205656; Churnetski et al. (2025), DOI: 10.1063/5.0268312.

title: Radiation-hard optical diagnostics
open: Maintain optical transmission, calibration, alignment, and detector performance over reactor neutron exposure and contamination.
status: ITER research plans retain diagnostic development needs; power-plant lifetime requirements are more demanding than laboratory access.
why: Gradual diagnostic drift can silently corrupt control and safety decisions.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Long-duration microwave diagnostic calibration
open: Preserve density and magnetic-field inference despite changing wall conditions, reflections, vibration, and inaccessible calibration paths.
status: Microwave diagnostics are established; autonomous long-duration calibration remains an operational qualification problem.
why: Reactor operation cannot rely on frequent manual recalibration.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005; Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*.

title: Real-time current-profile inference
open: Infer internal current and safety-factor profiles accurately enough for control using a reactor-feasible diagnostic set.
status: Magnetic control and integrated analysis frameworks exist; internal-profile ambiguity remains a limiting inverse problem.
why: Many dangerous instabilities depend on quantities that external sensors do not directly measure.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-29890-0.

title: Certified safe learned plasma control
open: Provide experimentally supported safety guarantees for learned controllers under model error, distribution shift, sensor failure, and actuator saturation.
status: Reinforcement learning controlled TCV plasmas in 2022 and avoided tearing instability in 2024; certification under reactor conditions remains open.
why: Good average performance is insufficient for a high-consequence control system.

title: Counterfactual disruption-control benchmarks
open: Build benchmarks that distinguish predicting disruption from actually preventing it, with defensible treatment of intervention and selection bias.
status: Prediction and avoidance demonstrations exist; observational labels alone cannot establish a controller’s causal benefit.
why: Successful interventions remove the very events a naive benchmark expects to observe.

title: Diagnostic-degradation-aware control
open: Detect and accommodate biased, drifting, intermittently missing, or radiation-damaged measurements without unsafe control actions.
status: Learned plasma control has experimental success; systematic degradation handling remains a separate reactor requirement.
why: Sensor failure need not look like an obvious outage.
key_works: Degrave et al. (2022), *Magnetic control of tokamak plasmas through deep reinforcement learning*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9; Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005.

title: Integrated multi-actuator planning
open: Coordinate heating, current drive, fueling, impurities, shape, and exhaust while accounting for conflicting objectives and different response times.
status: Individual control capabilities are established; complete reactor-wide constrained control remains unresolved.
why: Independent controllers can issue mutually incompatible actions.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; Degrave et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9.

title: Verifiable cyber-resilient fusion control
open: Establish a threat model, isolation architecture, and testable recovery guarantees for networked plasma, fuel-cycle, and plant controllers.
status: This is a proposed fusion-specific qualification problem built on existing industrial-control and emerging learned-control architectures.
why: Cyber faults must not defeat physical protection or create unsafe coordinated actions.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Predictive whole-plasma multiscale simulation
open: Simulate the coupled core, pedestal, scrape-off layer, neutrals, impurities, and evolving equilibrium with sufficient fidelity and practical computational cost.
status: Specialized models are powerful; no single validated calculation resolves every relevant scale and regime.
why: Reactor performance depends on interactions across model boundaries.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*; Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*.

title: Conservative kinetic–fluid interfaces
open: Couple kinetic and fluid descriptions across changing collisionality without introducing spurious particle, momentum, energy, or entropy behavior.
status: Both model classes are established; trustworthy interfaces remain a general unresolved numerical challenge.
why: Interface errors can masquerade as physical transport.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002; Giacomin and Ricci (2020), *Investigation of turbulent transport regimes in the tokamak edge by using two-fluid simulations*.

title: Whole-device uncertainty propagation
open: Propagate correlated uncertainties from nuclear data, material properties, transport models, controls, and manufacturing into plant performance and safety.
status: Integrated modeling frameworks exist, but a calibrated end-to-end uncertainty budget remains unavailable for most proposed plants.
why: Independent conservative margins can be wasteful, while ignored correlations can be dangerous.

title: Cross-code verification with analytic three-dimensional equilibria
open: Establish benchmark suites that reveal equilibrium-code errors in nonaxisymmetric, sheared-transform, and nonstandard-symmetry cases.
status: September 2026 analytic equilibria provide new exact tests; benchmark adoption and systematic code comparison remain open.
why: Agreement between two numerical codes is weaker evidence when they share assumptions or bugs.
key_works: Landreman (2026), *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces*, arXiv:2609.26742.

title: Open negative-result fusion datasets
open: Publish representative failed shots, unsuccessful materials, and rejected operating regimes with sufficient metadata for reproducible analysis.
status: Existing public data systems are valuable but do not guarantee unbiased coverage of failures; this is a proposed infrastructure target.
why: Success-biased datasets distort model training and feasibility assessment.
key_works: Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*; Ida (2023), associated LHD data DOI: 10.57451/lhd.analyzed-data.

title: Cross-device data semantics and provenance
open: Make experimental and simulated data interoperable with explicit units, calibration, uncertainty, geometry, processing history, and access rights.
status: IMAS already supplies a machine-generic framework; the open problem is complete adoption and semantic fidelity, not inventing the first schema.
why: Superficially compatible files can still encode incompatible physical meanings.
key_works: Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006.

title: Comparable cross-concept performance reporting
open: Establish auditable reporting that distinguishes target gain, plasma gain, engineering gain, pulse energy, duty factor, uncertainty, and externally maintained distributions.
status: Lawson-based surveys improve comparison; complete-system reporting remains less standardized than isolated plasma metrics.
why: Inconsistent boundaries can make incomparable experiments look directly competitive.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; Wurzel and Hsu (2025), arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Out-of-distribution materials benchmarks
open: Evaluate predictive materials models on unseen irradiation conditions, alloy families, processing routes, and laboratories rather than random splits of similar samples.
status: Materials-informatics opportunities exist; reactor-relevant generalization requires more demanding validation.
why: Interpolation accuracy can badly overstate qualification usefulness.
key_works: Hosemann et al. (2018), *Materials selection for nuclear applications*; Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.

title: Identifiable multimodal ICF reconstruction
open: Determine which hot-spot properties are uniquely recoverable from available diagnostics and report calibrated ambiguity where they are not.
status: Neural and multimodal reconstructions have advanced in 2024–2025; visually plausible reconstruction does not establish identifiability.
why: Incorrectly certain reconstructions can misdirect target optimization.

title: Hundredfold faster validated fusion prediction
open: Achieve a proposed 100× reduction in end-to-end prediction cost while preserving specified error bounds and detecting out-of-domain inputs.
status: Surrogates and integrated models exist; this target requires validation of complete decision quality, not only inference speed.
why: It could make uncertainty-aware reactor optimization and real-time planning practical.
key_works: Imbeaux et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006; Yang et al. (2026), *Multiscale Assessment of Tritium Behavior…Using Surrogate Models in TMAP8*, arXiv:2604.19647.

title: Hot-cell throughput
open: Process activated components through receipt, inspection, repair, detritiation, storage, and disposal fast enough to avoid becoming the maintenance bottleneck.
status: Remote-maintenance studies quantify major outage tasks; complete hot-cell logistics remain an important plant-level constraint.
why: Fast in-vessel replacement is insufficient if removed parts block the processing chain.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant, based on the EFDA WP12 pre-conceptual studies*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; arXiv:1412.4008.

title: Rapid remote divertor replacement
open: Demonstrate complete removal, replacement, reconnection, inspection, and recommissioning of representative activated divertor modules.
status: DEMO studies estimate substantial maintenance durations; these are planning estimates, not demonstrated reactor turnaround records.
why: Divertor replacement frequency may dominate capacity factor.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038.

title: Remotely qualified pressure-boundary reconnection
open: Reconnect coolant and vacuum boundaries remotely with verified leak tightness, structural integrity, inspectability, and repeatability.
status: Maintenance concepts exist; reactor-service qualification of repeated remote connections remains unresolved.
why: A single inaccessible leak can extend an outage dramatically.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: In-service inspection of activated structures
open: Detect consequential cracks, thinning, delamination, and coolant problems without dismantling the plant or exposing personnel.
status: Fusion materials qualification identifies lifetime uncertainty; reactor-compatible inspection is needed to manage it operationally.
why: Reliable inspection can permit safe operation without excessively conservative replacement.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: High-availability primary-loop machinery
open: Qualify pumps, valves, seals, bearings, and instrumentation for radioactive or reactive coolant loops with realistic maintenance access.
status: Blanket studies identify thermofluid requirements; industrial-duty machinery remains a separate qualification layer.
why: Conventional-looking balance-of-plant components can still become fusion-specific bottlenecks.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Pulse-to-steady power conversion
open: Smooth pulsed fusion heat and electrical demand into useful grid output with quantified storage losses, fatigue, and economics.
status: Pulsed and steady-state concepts are both studied; plant-specific buffering and cycling penalties remain unresolved.
why: The grid and turbine do not necessarily tolerate the plasma’s preferred waveform.
key_works: Schwartz et al. (2023), *The value of fusion energy to a decarbonized United States electric grid*, DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006; Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Tritium-isolating power-cycle heat exchangers
open: Transfer useful high-temperature heat while keeping tritium leakage, corrosion, pressure drop, and inspection burdens acceptable.
status: Blanket and tritium studies identify these coupled constraints; an integrated reactor-qualified solution remains open.
why: Contamination can spread from a compact nuclear island into a large conventional power system.
key_works: Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Practical charged-particle direct conversion
open: Convert a useful charged-particle energy distribution to electricity with acceptable efficiency, lifetime, contamination tolerance, and auxiliary power.
status: Direct conversion is attractive for several alternative concepts; complete reactor-duty performance remains unestablished.
why: It could bypass some thermal-cycle losses but introduces demanding particle-handling hardware.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Evidence-based fusion availability models
open: Replace largely assumed component failure and repair rates with traceable measurements, dependence models, and validated plant-level availability predictions.
status: Maintenance-duration studies and pilot-plant analyses exist; operating-fleet reliability data do not yet underpin them.
why: Availability assumptions can dominate electricity-cost estimates.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Safe black start, shutdown, and recovery
open: Demonstrate complete plant transitions through power loss, emergency shutdown, restart, and prolonged standby without unsafe inventory or thermal states.
status: Plasma control and plant roadmaps address constituent systems; integrated recovery behavior remains a qualification objective.
why: A plant must remain safe when its normal power and control assumptions fail.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Auditable fusion capital-cost models
open: Build cost estimates tied to actual quantities, manufacturing processes, labor, construction sequence, contingency, and uncertainty rather than aspirational unit costs.
status: Systems and grid-value models exist; first-of-a-kind cost credibility remains unresolved.
why: Physics feasibility does not determine whether a plant can be financed.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Schwartz et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006.

title: Availability–lifetime–cost optimum
open: Determine the economically optimal combination of operating intensity, component lifetime, replacement frequency, and reserve capacity.
status: Maintenance estimates and electricity-system models exist, but their coupled optimization lacks reactor operating evidence.
why: Maximizing instantaneous fusion power may increase the cost of delivered electricity.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008; Schwartz et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006.

title: Fusion construction learning curves
open: Determine which fusion costs can decline through repetition and which remain constrained by materials, site work, regulation, or physics.
status: No commercial operating fleet supplies an empirical fusion learning curve; current claims are prospective.
why: Fleet economics cannot safely assume solar-like or aircraft-like cost reductions without evidence.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*; Hsu et al. (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program…*, arXiv:2609.28398.

title: Fusion value in diverse future grids
open: Determine fusion’s value across regions, renewable mixes, storage costs, transmission limits, reliability standards, and alternative firm technologies.
status: A 2023 study provides detailed U.S. modeling and public data; its conditional results are not universal price forecasts.
why: An economically useful plant specification depends on the system into which it sells power.
key_works: Schwartz et al. (2023), *The value of fusion energy to a decarbonized United States electric grid*, DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006; dataset DOI: 10.34770/f8em-3c49.

title: Fleet-scale resource and lifecycle accounting
open: Quantify lithium, beryllium, helium, superconductors, structural materials, energy inputs, water, waste, and replacement flows for realistic deployment pathways.
status: Individual material and fuel constraints are studied; a harmonized uncertainty-aware fleet account remains incomplete.
why: A technology’s laboratory footprint can differ greatly from its fleet-scale footprint.
key_works: Pearson et al. (2018), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Competitive fusion process heat
open: Identify and demonstrate industrial heat applications whose temperature, availability, contamination barriers, and economics match achievable fusion systems.
status: Electricity dominates many roadmaps; non-electric applications require their own integration and market evidence.
why: Some industrial uses may value heat differently from an electricity grid.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Quantitative integrated fusion safety cases
open: Validate accident models that couple tritium, activated materials, chemical energy, magnetic energy, coolant behavior, and confinement failures.
status: Regulatory frameworks are advancing; plant-specific evidence remains necessary.
why: No single hazard category captures the full plant.
key_works: U.S. NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, proposed rule, Federal Register document 2026-03865; Abdou et al. (2015).

title: Tritium environmental-transfer uncertainty
open: Reduce uncertainty in site-relevant atmospheric, water, soil, and biological transport following routine and abnormal releases.
status: Tritium management is established, but environmental consequences depend on chemical form, local conditions, and exposure pathways.
why: Credible release limits require credible transport and dose models.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; NRC (2026), proposed fusion rule.

title: Activated-material recycling pathways
open: Establish technically and regulatorily acceptable routes for recycling or clearing activated fusion materials, with validated impurity and exposure accounting.
status: Reduced activation is a design objective, not a guarantee that all components qualify for unrestricted recycling.
why: Waste pathways affect material choice, cost, public acceptance, and decommissioning.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.

title: Common-cause and compound hazards
open: Analyze and test credible combinations such as power loss plus coolant failure, magnet faults plus structural motion, or fire plus tritium release.
status: Component protection does not establish resilience to correlated failures; integrated qualification remains open.
why: Independent safety layers can fail together when they share power, cooling, software, or physical space.
key_works: NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, proposed rule; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Fusion-specific evidence standards for licensing
open: Define accepted validation, uncertainty, inspection, and operational evidence for novel fusion components and machine classes.
status: The NRC published a proposed fusion-machine rule on February 26, 2026; the gap is not “no regulatory work exists.”
why: Developers and regulators need predictable standards for demonstrating safety.
key_works: U.S. NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, Federal Register document 2026-03865.

title: Qualified fusion component standards
open: Establish interoperable design and manufacturing standards for fusion-specific pressure boundaries, irradiation limits, remote joints, and functional materials.
status: Existing industrial and nuclear standards provide foundations; fusion-specific qualification remains incomplete.
why: Bespoke qualification for every plant slows deployment and fragments supply chains.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NRC (2026), proposed fusion-machine rule.

title: Evidence-based decommissioning provision
open: Estimate and validate decommissioning methods, waste volumes, tritium cleanup, schedules, and financial reserves for actual fusion architectures.
status: Materials and activation analyses inform planning; no commercial fusion fleet supplies realized decommissioning costs.
why: Underfunded end-of-life obligations can shift private project costs onto others.
key_works: NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.

title: Sustained funding for irradiation qualification
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Fund and operate shared irradiation and post-irradiation examination capacity with schedules aligned to component-development decisions.
status: The 2026 DOE roadmap identifies enabling infrastructure, but roadmap publication is not equivalent to secured multiyear appropriations.
why: Qualification bottlenecks can delay many otherwise independent fusion approaches.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*.

title: Shared integrated blanket test loops
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Provide accessible facilities combining relevant coolant chemistry, magnetic fields, heat flux, instrumentation, and component-scale geometry.
status: Specialized loops such as MaPLE exist; comprehensive shared coverage of coupled conditions remains incomplete.
why: Individual companies cannot efficiently duplicate every enabling experiment.
key_works: Smolentsev, ORNL research profile and MaPLE program; Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*.

title: Public-interest access to pilot-plant evidence
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Define agreements that make publicly supported performance, safety, failure, and qualification evidence reusable while protecting legitimate proprietary information.
status: Public–private milestone programs exist; evidence-sharing arrangements remain a policy-design problem.
why: Public investment should generate transferable knowledge rather than only isolated company assets.
key_works: Hsu, Wurzel, and Subramanian (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program of the U.S. Department of Energy*, arXiv:2609.28398.

title: Tritium reserve and allocation governance
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Establish transparent ownership, reserve, allocation, and contingency arrangements for scarce startup tritium across research and commercial users.
status: Supply constraints are documented; technical breeding projections do not settle allocation during shortages.
why: Uncoordinated procurement can strand projects or undermine shared research.
key_works: Pearson et al. (2018), *Tritium supply and use: a key issue for the development of nuclear fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.

title: Milestone funding without continuity failures
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Design funding mechanisms that preserve rigorous milestones while avoiding destructive gaps between technically interdependent development stages.
status: The September 2026 retrospective analyzes implementation experience of the DOE milestone program.
why: Stop–start financing can destroy teams and supply chains even when technical progress is real.
key_works: Hsu et al. (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program…*, arXiv:2609.28398.

title: First-plant financing and insurability
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Allocate construction, performance, technology, fuel, and decommissioning risks in a financing structure that is investable without hiding unbounded public liabilities.
status: Pilot-plant strategies exist; commercial underwriting lacks operating-fleet evidence.
why: A technically credible design can still fail to reach construction.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*; Hsu et al. (2026), arXiv:2609.28398.

title: Fusion qualification workforce
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Build sufficient expertise in tritium operations, remote handling, irradiation testing, nuclear quality assurance, superconducting fabrication, and plant commissioning.
status: The 2026 DOE roadmap explicitly includes workforce development; specialized capacity cannot be created by general hiring alone.
why: Shared shortages can delay an entire industry.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Falsifiable funding for underexplored concepts
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Create competitive support for non-mainstream fusion approaches tied to decisive, independently interpretable experiments rather than indefinite promise or premature exclusion.
status: Cross-concept gain surveys show diverse development levels; funding design must distinguish uncertainty from evidence of failure.
why: It preserves useful exploration while limiting uninformative expenditure.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Fusion propulsion with credible specific power
open: Demonstrate a complete propulsion architecture whose thrust, specific impulse, reactor mass, shielding, heat rejection, and auxiliary power close simultaneously.
status: NASA and other groups have published fusion-propulsion concepts; concept-level performance is not integrated propulsion evidence.
why: Space applications may value fusion differently, but mass and waste heat replace grid economics as dominant constraints.
key_works: NASA (2012), *Z-Pinch Magneto-Inertial Fusion Propulsion Engine Design Concept*, NTRS:20120016553.

title: Efficient fusion magnetic nozzles
open: Convert fusion-plasma energy into directed exhaust while controlling detachment, divergence, electron losses, magnetic reaction forces, and hardware exposure.
status: Fusion-propulsion concepts require such conversion; complete reactor-compatible nozzle performance remains unresolved.
why: Producing energetic plasma is not equivalent to producing useful thrust.
key_works: NASA (2012), *Z-Pinch Magneto-Inertial Fusion Propulsion Engine Design Concept*, NTRS:20120016553.

title: Tenfold faster activated-component replacement
open: Achieve a proposed 10× reduction in complete replacement outage time relative to a specified, reproducible baseline, including inspection and recommissioning.
status: DEMO maintenance studies provide explicit baseline estimates; the target is not satisfied by speeding up only one robotic motion.
why: Maintenance innovation could improve economics without requiring better plasma confinement.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; arXiv:1412.4008.

title: Hundredfold faster component qualification
open: Achieve a proposed 100× reduction in qualification time or experimental burden for a defined component class while retaining independently validated lifetime and safety confidence.
status: Accelerated testing, multiscale models, and surrogates offer ingredients; equivalent confidence is the unresolved requirement.
why: Qualification speed may matter as much as invention speed for deployment.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Transport-time validity of nonlinear gyrokinetics
open: Establish error bounds between full kinetic dynamics and nonlinear gyrokinetics over transport times, including evolving profiles, collisions, and electromagnetic fluctuations. The bound should identify when apparently small ordering errors accumulate into consequential heat or particle flux errors.
status: Systematic gyrokinetic reductions and conservation laws are established; a formal ordering is not a uniform, reactor-geometry, transport-time error guarantee.
why: This would distinguish trustworthy extrapolation from agreement obtained within an uncontrolled approximation.
key_works: Brizard and Hahm (2007), *Foundations of nonlinear gyrokinetic theory*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.79.421.

title: Gauge-consistent truncation with evolving equilibrium
open: Construct practical electromagnetic gyrokinetic truncations that retain gauge consistency and the correct energy exchange when equilibrium fields and distribution functions evolve on transport timescales.
status: Variational formulations supply important consistency conditions. Combining changing backgrounds, numerical truncation, and practical field solvers remains more demanding than deriving a fixed-order continuum model.
why: Small inconsistencies can generate artificial heating or apparent momentum transport.
key_works: Brizard and Hahm (2007), *Foundations of nonlinear gyrokinetic theory*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.79.421.

title: Gyrokinetic ordering through the steepest pedestal regions
open: Determine where pedestal gradients, strong electric-field shear, and finite orbit widths invalidate conventional gyrokinetic ordering, and construct a validated replacement or matching procedure there.
status: Peripheral-plasma models extend gyrokinetics to stronger flows and non-Maxwellian distributions, but retain explicit scale-separation assumptions.
why: The region controlling global confinement may also be where a favored approximation is least secure.
key_works: Frei, Jorge, and Ricci (2019 preprint), *A gyrokinetic model for the plasma periphery of tokamak devices*, arXiv:1904.06863.

title: Uniform kinetic-to-collisional moment closure
open: Develop an adaptive moment hierarchy that remains accurate across collisionless core-like conditions and highly collisional peripheral plasma without changing the physical model by hand.
status: Gyro-moment formulations provide a systematic hierarchy. Selecting and closing a small, sufficient set of moments throughout a changing discharge remains an unresolved reduction problem.
why: A reliable adaptive hierarchy could make whole-plasma kinetic calculations substantially more practical.
key_works: Frei, Jorge, and Ricci (2019), *A gyrokinetic model for the plasma periphery of tokamak devices*, arXiv:1904.06863.

title: Affordable full nonlinear Coulomb collisions
open: Implement the full nonlinear gyrokinetic Coulomb operator at production scale without replacing important velocity-space structure by uncontrolled model collisions.
status: The nonlinear operator has already been derived; the open problem is computationally affordable use in demanding electromagnetic, multispecies simulations.
why: Collision-model choices can influence transport thresholds, impurity behavior, and irreversible heating.
key_works: Jorge, Frei, and Ricci (2019), *Nonlinear Gyrokinetic Coulomb Collision Operator*, arXiv:1906.03252.

title: Reactive collisions with changing charge states
open: Couple gyrokinetic Coulomb collisions to ionization, recombination, and charge exchange while preserving the appropriate particle, momentum, and total-energy balances across changing species populations.
status: A nonlinear Coulomb operator alone does not supply the reactive collision system required for partially ionized edge plasmas.
why: Incorrect source coupling can create artificial energy or impurity transport near the plasma boundary.
key_works: Jorge, Frei, and Ricci (2019), *Nonlinear Gyrokinetic Coulomb Collision Operator*, arXiv:1906.03252; Osborne et al. (2024–2025), arXiv:2410.14403.

title: Conservation and positivity under adaptive remeshing
open: Preserve positivity, conservation, and the discrete entropy law when collision calculations are combined with velocity-grid adaptation, spatial remeshing, and transfers between kinetic representations.
status: Discretizations satisfying these properties already exist for the nonlinear Landau operator. The unresolved extension is maintaining them through the additional operations used by practical adaptive simulations.
why: Remeshing should not introduce negative populations or erase physically important tails.
key_works: Hirvijoki, Burby, and Kraus (2018), *Energy-, momentum-, density-, and positivity-preserving spatio-temporal discretizations for the nonlinear Landau collision operator with exact H-theorems*, arXiv:1804.08546.

title: Cancellation control during reconnection
open: Demonstrate that electromagnetic particle schemes retain accurate parallel electric fields during reconnection and other departures from ideal Ohm’s law, at realistic mass ratio and low collisionality.
status: Generalized mixed-variable pullback methods reported in 2025 address nonideal Ohm’s law; simple verification cases do not establish nonlinear reconnection accuracy.
why: Numerical cancellation errors can masquerade as the electric fields responsible for topology change.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *Generalized mixed variable-pullback scheme with non-ideal Ohm’s law for electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations*, arXiv:2509.19553.

title: Pullback frequency versus statistical noise
